title: PostgreSQL Small Examples
description: Use these small PostgreSQL examples with the tools described in each lesson. Read the expected result before you try a change.

examples.title: Ask the database a question
examples.description: A SELECT query can calculate a value without reading a table.
examples.output: The result is one row with total_books equal to 5.

examples.title: Make a practice table
examples.description: A table names the facts each row can hold.
examples.output: A temporary book table exists for the current database session. Each new row must have a title and a positive page count.

examples.title: Return an inserted value
examples.description: RETURNING asks PostgreSQL to show values from a row it has just changed.
examples.output: The inserted row is shown with its generated id and Moon Trip title.

examples.title: Search text without letter case
examples.description: ILIKE is PostgreSQL's case-insensitive pattern match.
examples.code:
WITH books(title) AS (VALUES ('Moon Trip'),('Garden Days'))
SELECT title FROM books WHERE title ILIKE 'moon%';
examples.output: The result contains Moon Trip even though the pattern begins with lowercase moon.

examples.title: Sort before taking a few rows
examples.description: ORDER BY chooses the result order. LIMIT then restricts how many of those rows are returned.
examples.code:
WITH books(title,pages) AS (VALUES ('Moon Trip',60),('Garden Days',40),('Tiny Seed',20))
SELECT title,pages FROM books ORDER BY pages,title LIMIT 2;
examples.output: Tiny Seed appears first, then Garden Days.

examples.title: Count rows in each group
examples.description: GROUP BY puts matching values together. An aggregate such as count gives one answer for each group.
examples.code:
WITH books(kind) AS (VALUES ('story'),('science'),('story'))
SELECT kind,count(*) AS book_count FROM books GROUP BY kind ORDER BY kind;
examples.output: Science has 1 book and story has 2.

examples.title: Join related facts
examples.description: A join matches rows using a shared value.
examples.output: The row pairs Moon Trip with Mia.

examples.title: Keep a change in a transaction
examples.description: A transaction groups changes into one job.
examples.output: The final count is 0 because the insert was rolled back.

examples.title: Read a JSONB field
examples.description: JSONB stores JSON data in a form PostgreSQL can query.
examples.output: The title column contains Moon Trip.

examples.title: Use an array for a small value list
examples.description: PostgreSQL can store an array of values.
examples.output: The result is true because science is in the array.

examples.title: Number rows without grouping them
examples.description: A window function calculates across related rows while keeping each row visible.
examples.code:
WITH books(title,pages) AS (VALUES ('Moon Trip',60),('Tiny Seed',20))
SELECT title,row_number() OVER (ORDER BY pages,title) AS reading_order FROM books ORDER BY reading_order;
examples.output: Tiny Seed gets 1 and Moon Trip gets 2.

examples.title: Read a query plan first
examples.description: EXPLAIN shows how PostgreSQL plans to run a query.
examples.code: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM pg_books WHERE id=1;
examples.output: The plan describes a possible access method for the practice table. Exact details depend on its size and statistics.
